pos: n. (a defamatory writing or picture published to bring a man into contempt)
etymology: Latin libellus, a little book, from liber, a book. Webster: any book, pamphlet, writing, or picture, maliciously made or published, tending to bring a person into contempt or expose him to public hatred.
biblical_def:
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour. He that uttereth a slander is a fool. The man who dwells with God backbiteth not with his tongue, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour. Every idle word shall be given account of in the day of judgment.

A libel is a slander put in writing or in a picture and handed to another. The pen does not make the sin lighter. It makes the wound travel. Scripture judges the false witness whether the lie is spoken in a gate or printed on a page.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a defamatory writing; any book, pamphlet, writing, or picture maliciously published to bring a person into contempt or public hatred. In a wider sense, any blasphemous, treasonable, or immoral writing made public.
webster_full: LIBEL, n. A defamatory writing. Any book, pamphlet, writing or picture, containing representations, maliciously made or published, tending to bring a person into contempt, or expose him to public hatred and derision.
The communication of such defamatory writing to a single person is considered in law a publication.
In a more extensive sense, any blasphemous, treasonable or immoral writing or picture made public is a libel.
scriptures: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
He that hideth hatred with lying lips, and he that uttereth a slander, is a fool.
Psa 15:3
He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour.
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
corruption_summary: The age treats a printed attack as commentary, so that a false witness becomes content once it has an audience.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster already says the communication of a defamatory writing to a single person is publication. A private message that carries a lie about a neighbour is not less a libel because it never saw a press.
The corruption is the habit of calling the writing brave. Scripture calls the uttering of a slander folly, and it will require an account of the idle word.
roots_summary: Latin libellus, a little book. The moral field is false witness (Exo 20:16) and slander (Pro 10:18).
roots_lines: The little book is the point. A short writing can do the work of a long accusation.
Psalm 15:3 refuses both the backbiting tongue and the taken-up reproach. A libel is the reproach made portable.
usage: Thou shalt not bear false witness — the commandment under every published attack.
Every idle word — the day of judgment does not exempt the printed page.

pos: n. (irreverence of sacred things; the taking of God's name in vain)
etymology: From profane, Latin profanus, outside the temple. Webster defines profanity as profaneness: irreverence of sacred things, particularly language that implies irreverence toward God, the taking of God's name in vain.
biblical_def:
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain. Ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God. The prayer the Lord taught begins the other way: Hallowed be thy name.

Profanity is speech that drags the holy into the common, and especially speech that spends the Name as an oath, a joke, or a curse. The guilt is not in the volume of the voice. It is in the use of the Name as if it belonged to the speaker.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under profaneness: irreverence of sacred things; particularly, the use of language which implies irreverence towards God; the taking of God's name in vain.
webster_full: PROFANITY, n. Profaneness.
PROFANENESS, n. Irreverence of sacred things; particularly, the use of language which implies irreverence towards God; the taking of God's name in vain.
scriptures: Exo 20:7
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
And ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the LORD.
Mat 6:9
After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
corruption_summary: The age calls profanity strong language, as if the sin were a matter of taste rather than a theft of the Name.
corruption_paragraphs: The third commandment does not wait for a courtroom oath. It forbids taking the Name in vain, and it adds that the LORD will not hold that man guiltless.
Hallowed be thy name is the opposite sentence. A mouth trained on profanity cannot pray that line without repenting of the other use.
roots_summary: Latin profanus, before or outside the temple. The biblical charge is taking the Name in vain (Exo 20:7) and profaning it (Lev 19:12).
roots_lines: Profane speech puts holy things outside the temple and into the street as common coin.
Matthew 6:9 is the repair: the Name is to be hallowed, not spent.
usage: Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain — the commandment profanity breaks.
Hallowed be thy name — the prayer that cannot share a mouth with a curse.

pos: n. (a pledge of goods given as security for money borrowed)
etymology: Latin pignus, a pledge. Webster applies pawn only to goods, chattels, or money, not to real estate. To pawn is to deposit that security, or to pledge one's word.
biblical_def:
When thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge. Thou shalt stand abroad, and the man to whom thou dost lend shall bring out the pledge abroad unto thee. Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts. My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger, Scripture has already begun the warning.

A pawn is a pledge. The law protects the poor man's house from the lender who would walk in and take it. The pledge may be brought out. The threshold may not be crossed. To pawn one's word is a heavier deposit than a coat, because the word is the man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): something given or deposited as security for the payment of money borrowed; a pledge. Applied only to goods, chattels, or money, not to real estate. Also a pledge for the fulfillment of a promise.
webster_full: PAWN, n. Something given or deposited as security for the payment of money borrowed; a pledge. Pawn is applied only to goods, chattels or money, and not to real estate.
A pledge for the fulfillment of a promise.
To pawn: to give or deposit in pledge, or as security for the payment of money borrowed.
scriptures: When thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge.
Thou shalt stand abroad, and the man to whom thou dost lend shall bring out the pledge abroad unto thee.
Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts.
Pro 6:1
My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger,
corruption_summary: The age treats a pawn shop as ordinary commerce and forgets that the pledge was meant to protect the poor, not to strip his house.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 24 does not forbid a pledge. It forbids the lender entering the house to fetch it. The poor man brings the pledge out. That limit is the difference between a loan and a raid.

To pawn one's honor, which Webster also names, is the same shape in speech. A man deposits his word for a debt he may not be able to pay, and Proverbs has already told the son not to strike hands for debts.
roots_summary: Latin pignus, a pledge. The biblical word in Deuteronomy 24 is the pledge the lender may not fetch from inside the house.
roots_lines: The pledge stays a pledge. It does not become a license to cross the threshold.
Proverbs 6:1 and 22:26 set suretyship beside this danger. A struck hand can pawn a man as surely as a coat.
usage: Thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge — the limit on every pawn.
Be not thou one of them that are sureties for debts — the word pawned is harder to redeem than the goods.

pos: n. (the seizing and enjoying of another's place or property without right)
etymology: Latin usurpare, to seize for one's own use. Webster: the act of seizing or occupying and enjoying the property of another, without right; as the usurpation of a throne, or of the supreme power.
biblical_def:
I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence. Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel, standing in the way of judgment until the kingdom answered to his name rather than his father's.

Usurpation is the taking of an office, a throne, or an authority that was not given. It is not ambition that waits to be called. It is seizure. The word in 1 Timothy 2:12 is the apostolic refusal of a seized authority in the church. Absalom is the political exhibit: a son who enjoyed a rule he had not received.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of seizing or occupying and enjoying the property of another, without right; as the usurpation of a throne, or of the supreme power.
webster_full: USURPATION, n. The act of seizing or occupying and enjoying the property of another, without right.
As the usurpation of a throne; the usurpation of the supreme power.
scriptures: But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.
And on this manner did Absalom to all Israel that came to the king for judgment: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.
corruption_summary: The age calls a seized office empowerment, so that taking what was not given is praised as courage.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's without-right is the whole case. A calling that God has not given is not supplied by desire. Absalom wanted judgment. He stole hearts to get it.
First Timothy 2:12 uses the verb the English has long rendered usurp. The corruption is to treat that verb as a later insult rather than as Paul's own description of an authority taken, not received.
roots_summary: Greek authenteo (G831) in 1 Timothy 2:12, to assume a stance of authority. The narrative exhibit is Absalom's stolen hearts (2Sa 15:6).
roots_lines: Usurpation enjoys the place. That is Webster's second verb. Seizing is not enough. The usurper sits.
Absalom did not begin with a crown. He began with stolen hearts. The usurpation was already underway.
usage: Nor to usurp authority over the man — Paul's name for an office taken, not given.
Absalom stole the hearts — usurpation that starts in the gate, not on the throne.

pos: n. (the taking of something from another's reputation, from envy or malice)
etymology: Latin detractio, a taking away. Webster: the act of taking something from the reputation or worth of another, in order to lessen him; censure from envy or malice. If the imputation is false, it is slander.
biblical_def:
Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother speaketh evil of the law. He that goeth about as a talebearer revealeth secrets. He that backbiteth not with his tongue is the man who may abide in God's tabernacle.

Detraction is the diminishing of a brother's name. It may use a true fault, told to lessen him, or a false charge. Webster already marks the difference: false imputation is slander. Either way, the aim is the same. Something is taken from the man so that the speaker may stand taller.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of taking something from the reputation or worth of another, to lessen him in estimation; censure from envy or malice. If the imputation is false, it is slander or defamation.
webster_full: DETRACTION, n. The act of taking something from the reputation or worth of another, with the view to lessen him in estimation.
Detraction may consist in representing merit as less than it really is, or in the imputation of faults.
If such imputation is false, it is slander or defamation.
scriptures: Jas 4:11

Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law: but if thou judge the law, thou art not a doer of the law, but a judge.
He that goeth about as a talebearer revealeth secrets: therefore meddle not with him that flattereth with his lips.
Psa 15:3
He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour.
corruption_summary: The age calls detraction honesty, so that diminishing a brother is praised as telling it like it is.
corruption_paragraphs: James does not permit the evil speech because the fault was real. Speaking evil of a brother is speaking evil of the law. The detractor has left the place of a doer and taken the place of a judge.

Webster's distinction still helps. A false charge is slander. A true fault, carried about to lessen the man, is still detraction. Psalm 15 refuses both the backbiting tongue and the taken-up reproach.
roots_summary: Latin detrahere, to draw away. The biblical field is speaking evil of a brother (Jas 4:11) and backbiting (Psa 15:3).
roots_lines: Detraction draws something away from a name. The thing drawn is reputation. The motive Webster names is envy or malice.
James 4:11 puts the speaker on trial. The law is what he has judged.
usage: Speak not evil one of another — the apostolic ban on detraction.
He that backbiteth not with his tongue — the man fit for the tabernacle.

pos: n. (the officious or malicious carrying of tales and secrets)
etymology: English, from tale and bear. Webster: the act of informing officiously; communication of secrets maliciously. The talebearer is one who makes mischief by that officiousness.
biblical_def:
Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people. Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth. A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter.

Talebearing is the trade of carrying another man's matter where it will burn. The law forbids the going up and down. The proverb names the result. Strife needs wood. The talebearer is the wood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of informing officiously; communication of secrets maliciously.
webster_full: TALEBEARING, n. The act of informing officiously; communication of secrets maliciously.
TALEBEARER, n. A person who officiously tells tales; one who makes mischief in society by his officiousness.
scriptures: Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD.
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter.
corruption_summary: The age calls talebearing transparency, so that carrying a secret into the street is treated as a public service.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 19:16 sets talebearing beside standing against the blood of a neighbour. The carried tale is not a small social sin. It can become a witness against a man's life.
A faithful spirit conceals the matter. That is not a cover for crime. It is the refusal to spend another man's secret as fuel. Where the talebearer is removed, the proverb says the strife goes out.
roots_summary: Hebrew rakil (H7400), a slanderer, talebearer, the one who goes about. Leviticus 19:16 and Proverbs 11:13.
roots_lines: The Hebrew pictures a going about. Talebearing is a walk, not a single sentence.
Proverbs 26:20 makes the talebearer the wood. Remove the carrier and the fire fails.
usage: Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer — the statute.
Where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth — the proverb's cure.

pos: n. (a trader who cannot pay his just debts, or who acts to defraud his creditors)
etymology: Likely bank-broken, the fund broken, with Latin ruptus, broken. Webster's strict sense is a trader who secretes himself or otherwise tends to defraud his creditors. In the looser sense, a trader unable to pay his just debts. He does not apply the word to every insolvent man.
biblical_def:
The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth. The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender. Scripture does not use the statute-word. It does name the man whose debts outrun his payment, and it names the wickedness of borrowing with no intent to pay.

A bankrupt, in Webster's strict sense, is a trader. The moral question underneath the statute is older: does the man pay what he owes, or does he hide? Inability is not the same act as fraud. Both can break a fund. Only one is the wickedness of Psalm 37.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a trader who secretes himself, or does certain other acts tending to defraud his creditors; in a looser sense, a trader unable to pay his just debts. Bankruptcy belongs to traders; insolvency, to other persons.
webster_full: BANKRUPT, n. A trader who secretes himself, or does certain other acts tending to defraud his creditors.
In a less technical sense, a trader who fails or becomes unable to pay his just debts.
In strictness, no person but a trader can be a bankrupt. Bankruptcy is applied to merchants and traders; insolvency, to other persons.
scriptures: The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth.
Pro 22:7
The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.
Rom 13:8
Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law.
corruption_summary: The age uses bankrupt as a sneer for any empty purse, and also as a costume for the man who hides from the debt.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster keeps the word on the trader, and he keeps fraud in the strict definition. A failed harvest is not the same as a secreted self. Psalm 37:21 judges the second.

The other corruption is the boast. A man calls himself bankrupt to end the conversation about what he still owes. The borrower remains servant to the lender until the debt is paid or forgiven by the one who holds it.
roots_summary: Latin ruptus, broken. The moral field is the wicked who pays not again (Psa 37:21) and the borrower as servant (Pro 22:7).
roots_lines: The broken bank is the picture. The fund failed. The duty to the creditor did not.
Webster's limit matters. Not every poor man is a bankrupt. The word belongs to trade, and in its strict sense to fraud.
usage: The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again — the verse under the strict sense.
The borrower is servant to the lender — why the name is never a small insult.

pos: n. (a feast of noisy merriment; carousing)
etymology: From revel, to feast riotously. Webster: a feasting with noisy merriment; revelry. He points the reader to Galatians 5 and 1 Peter 4.
biblical_def:
Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. Peter names the time past, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries. That time, he says, may suffice.

Reveling is not a meal and not a wedding joy. It is the noisy feast that belongs with drunkenness and with the works that shut a man out of the kingdom. The apostle does not negotiate with it. He lists it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a feasting with noisy merriment; revelry. He cites Galatians 5 and 1 Peter 4.
webster_full: REVELING, n. A feasting with noisy merriment; revelry.
Webster points the word to Galatians 5 and 1 Peter 4.
scriptures: Gal 5:21
Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
corruption_summary: The age calls reveling a celebration, so that the feast Paul lists among the works of the flesh is sold as a good time.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 5:21 does not isolate reveling as a minor excess beside the real sins. It stands in the same list as drunkenness and murder, and the sentence is inheritance lost.
Peter's suffice us is the apostolic clock. The time past was enough. A church that schedules the revel and calls it fellowship has stopped reading the list.
roots_summary: Greek komos (G2970), a revel, carousal, the nocturnal riot. Galatians 5:21 and 1 Peter 4:3.
roots_lines: The Greek is not a feast of charity. It is the carousal.
Paul's and such like keeps the list open. Reveling is a kind, not a lone exception.
usage: They which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God — Paul's sentence on revellings.
The time past of our life may suffice us — Peter's refusal to extend the revel.
